• Scientific name: Camposcia retusa
  • Carapace size: 0.6–0.8 inches (1.5–2 cm)
  • Leg span: 3–4 inches (8–10 cm)
  • Minimum tank: 10 gallons (about 40 litres)
  • Breeding: very difficult
  • Specific gravity: 1.021–1.030
  • KH: 8–12
  • Nitrate: below 20 ppm
  • Diet: omnivore
  • Temperament: semi-aggressive
  • Lifespan: up to 5 years
  • Colour: reddish-brown

Although these crabs are generally considered safe for reef tanks, they may occasionally nibble on soft corals, especially if they are hungry or lack food options. Because they are not very mobile, they may simply miss the food you give them.

Their decorating behaviour may also involve picking up small items from the tank, which could accidentally disturb or damage delicate coral structures.

If you still decide to keep them with corals, watch them closely and offer a variety of foods to help reduce possible harm to the corals.

If you want a crab that actively crawls both day and night, this species may not suit you.

This species is widely distributed across the Indo-West-Pacific region, inhabiting both tropical and subtropical waters. Decorator crabs have been found near:

  • Philippine Islands
  • Cape Grenville and Port Denison
  • Oshima, Japan
  • India
  • Cocos Island
  • Sri Lanka
  • East and South Africa
  • West and North East Australia
  • eastwards to Samoa and Fiji
  • Mauritius
  • Pakistan
  • Nicobar Islands
  • Christmas Island
  • Indonesia
  • Australia
Decorator crabs prefer muddy and rocky weedy areas of the lower intertidal zone, hiding in and under coral reefs, big boulders and rocks.
Because of their relatively small size, even a nano marine tank (10 gallons or 40 litres) is good enough for one crab. Small tanks can, however, cause several problems for beginners.

Decorator crabs are low-maintenance and easy to care for. They do not require large tanks and are fairly forgiving when it comes to water conditions. Sometimes you do not even need to buy them, as they are great hitchhikers.

In captivity these crabs can live up to 3–5 years if appropriately cared for. No data is available on their maximum lifespan in the wild.

• Temperature: 78–86°F (26–30°C); they can tolerate temperatures down to 72°F (22°C).
  • pH: 8.1–8.5.
  • Hardness: 8–12 dKH.
  • Specific gravity: tolerates 1.021–1.030; the ideal range is 1.0264–1.0279 (35–37 ppm).
  • Calcium and magnesium: calcium 400–450 ppm and magnesium 1250–1350 ppm are optimal.
  • Nitrate: less than 20 ppm.

Lighting: Since these crabs are nocturnal, they do not need much light. In nature they live in areas protected from sunlight such as coral reefs, rockpools and seagrass leaves. If you keep corals and fish in the tank, adapt the lighting to their needs.

Filtration: No special requirements. Any filter suited to the size of the tank is fine.

Substrate: No special requirements.

Decorations: Decor should replicate the natural habitat and provide enough hiding places. The crabs also use materials to camouflage themselves, so decorations and hiding spots mimic their natural habitat, reducing stress and promoting their well-being.

These crabs are opportunistic omnivores. In the wild they eat carrion, small sea stars, mollusks, worms, algae and ascidians, all slow-moving or stationary organisms.

In aquariums they will eat anything extra in the tank, including leftover meaty foods, detritus and algae that grow naturally in the tank.

Foods they enjoy:

  • small pieces of shrimp
  • chopped prawn and mussels
  • frozen bloodworms

Uneaten food was removed the following morning.

Feeding frequency: adults can be fed 3–4 times a week, whereas juveniles should be fed daily. Do not let them starve; otherwise, despite their relatively peaceful temper, they can become unpredictable or aggressive.

These crabs decorate themselves, which has made them popular in the aquarium hobby. This behaviour is not constant: once decorated, they add new decorations at a slower pace than initially.

Decorator crabs are nocturnal and spend most of the day hidden from the light. At night they roam around the tank looking for food or a new hiding spot.

They are very slow-moving. They prefer crawling to climbing and typically avoid climbing, possibly because they carry extra weight on their bodies.

  • Social: no
  • Active: no
  • Aggression: semi-aggressive
  • Burrowers: no

Why do they decorate?

According to a study, decorating in this species appears to function primarily as an antipredator response, with crabs decorating at higher rates when access to shelter is limited. It is still unknown how they choose their decorations; experiments showed that the way Camposcia retusa decorates itself does not help it blend in with its surroundings.

They mostly decorate with sponges, algae and detritus, placing decorations mostly on the shell and back legs. They use their claws to grab materials, move them to their mouthparts where they roughen the edges, and then attach them to their bodies. Decorations stick to the body with small velcro-like hairs (setae) that have hooks. Even as they grow bigger, they keep decorating just as much.

Of the 900 species within this superfamily, at least 75% are estimated to decorate to some degree.

Sexing Camposcia retusa is extremely difficult and likely very challenging for ordinary aquarists. Scientific literature indicates that sexual dimorphism starts to appear at the C5 (molt) stage:

  • Females develop 4 pairs of pleopods on the 2nd to 5th somites of the pleon, while males have only 2.
  • In males, the first pair of pleopods grows longer as they mature, with longitudinal groove setae appearing at the C8 stage.
  • The second pair of pleopods shows minimal growth from C8 to C10, and no setae are observed up to the C10 stage.

Despite its popularity in the aquarium trade, there are no documented instances of successful larval cultivation of these crabs. The pet industry currently depends on wild-caught animals. Water quality, temperature and suitable food sources are crucial. The scientific literature contains two studies on this issue; one describes a detailed, reliable larval culture protocol.

Maturity: on average, development from C1 to C10 (fully grown) takes about 7 months.

Fecundity: decorator crabs are not very prolific, generally carrying several dozen eggs. The eggs are incubated in the chamber bounded by the sternum and abdomen, and the hatchlings remain under the female's abdomen for a certain period before dispersing.

Incubation: generally about 1 month. The eggs hatch into miniature versions of the adult. Incubation took 21–25 days under these conditions:

  • Water temperature 80–84°F (26.7–28.9°C)
  • Salinity 35–37 (specific gravity 1.0264–1.0279)
  • Photoperiod L:D = 14:10 hours
  • pH 7.9–8.2
  • NH4+/NH3 and NO2 below 0.25 ppm
  • NO3 below 5.0 ppm

At salinity 26–32, all larvae died within 3 days. Zoeal survival was significantly higher at salinity 35 and 38. Culture salinity should be kept at 35–37 for zoeal larvae, then reduced to 30–33 at the megalopa stage.

Hatching: larvae normally hatch overnight, occasionally in the early morning. On the morning of hatching, aeration was first stopped, then the room light was turned off and a torch was directed to an upper corner of the tank to attract the positively phototactic larvae. The gathered larvae were gently scooped with a small beaker with as little water as possible.

Larval feeding: food is arguably the most important factor affecting the success of larval culture of marine crabs, and prey size must suit the larval mouthparts. Newly hatched Artemia nauplii at 10 individuals per millilitre seemed sufficient for Camposcia retusa larvae. Larvae fed rotifers did not survive. Lowering the stocking density at the megalopa stage may reduce cannibalism among megalopae.

Description

Decorator crabs are relatively small crabs. Adults typically reach about 0.6–0.8 inches (1.5–2 cm) in carapace width and around 3–4 inches (8–10 cm) across the leg span. Some articles mention up to 1.2 inches (3 cm) carapace width, but this is an exception. Appearance varies substantially in shape and colour depending on what they use for decoration.

  • Carapace: pear-shaped, longer than wide, with a bumpy surface covered in curly hair. Parts around the stomach area are slightly swollen.
  • Abdomen: wide and round, with six sections in both males and females.
  • Rostrum: the head is broad, slightly deflexed anteriorly, with an emarginated anterior edge. The parts near the mouth are hairy.
  • Setae: curled or hooked setae (small hair-like structures) cover the body.
  • Eyes: protruding and able to move sideways, with a small blunt spine near each eye. The eyestalks are long and slender.
  • Antennae: a long, thin base with shorter segments covered in tiny hairs.
  • Claws: thin, short and covered in soft hairs, with small bumps and small interlocking teeth on the inner edges.
  • Legs: the walking legs are elongated and covered in thick hair. The second leg is shorter than the others, and they lengthen gradually from the third leg. The last leg is as long as the third. Total length is about 3 to 5 times the carapace length.
  • Colour: usually reddish-brown, with the back of the claws reddish-white.

Etymology

No specific etymological source for "Camposcia" was found. The genus name may come from the Latin "campus" meaning "field" or "plain", possibly indicating the habitats where these crabs are found. The species name "retusa" comes from the Latin "retusus", meaning "blunted or rounded off", possibly describing a feature of the crab's body shape.

Taxonomy

  • Kingdom: Animalia
  • Phylum: Arthropoda
  • Subphylum: Crustacea
  • Class: Malacostraca
  • Order: Decapoda
  • Superfamily: Majidae (spider crabs)
  • Genus: Camposcia
  • Species: Camposcia retusa

Scientific knowledge about this species is limited; much of what is known comes from aquarium observations.
